title: Data modeling and metric contracts
summary: Declare the grain, build a star whose joins hold, keep history and missing keys honest, and write a metric contract that reconciles at three grains and catches five classic failures.
objectives: Declare the grain of a fact and a metric, separate facts from dimensions, and tell a medallion label from a modeled entity.
Join facts to conformed and type 2 dimensions with a known cardinality, keeping missing keys visible under an unknown member.
Write and test a metric contract that reconciles the unit defect rate at line-day, plant-day and plant-month and catches double counts, empty denominators, mixed units and calendar-day windows.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
Grain first: what one row means
Keys that hold: conformed, historical and missing
The contract, its platform home and the wide table
Worked example: North and South, 26 March to 1 April

questions.prompt: South's plant-day parts in March are 240 / 0, 300 / 15, 180 / 3 and 120 / 3 (inspected / defective pieces). What is South's March unit defect rate under the contract?

options.rationale: Correct: the month sums the plant-days' parts, 21 defective of 840 inspected, and divides once.
Averaging day rates weights a 120-piece day like a 300-piece day; the contract sums parts.
The worst day answers a different question; the monthly rate covers every inspected piece.

options.text: No rate, because 26 March had no defective pieces
options.rationale: Zero defective out of 240 inspected is a real 0% day, not an empty denominator.

questions.prompt: In April the silver inspections hold North 250, South 300 and 50 pieces on line N3, which has no dim_line row yet. An April report inner-joins them to dim_line on line_id and the validity window. Which inspected total does it show?

options.text: 550, and the 50 N3 pieces vanish without a message
options.rationale: Correct: an inner join keeps only matched rows, and N3 has no dimension row to match.

options.text: 600, because a join keeps every fact
options.rationale: An inner join is exactly the join that drops unmatched facts; a left join or unknown member keeps them.
Nothing duplicates N3; with no dimension row it matches zero times, not twice.
Joins do not report unmatched keys, which is why the lab lists orphans in a separate check.

questions.prompt: unit_defect_rate is defined in a metric view as MEASURE(defective_pieces) divided by MEASURE(inspected_pieces). A query groups by plant and month. How is North's March value produced?

options.rationale: Correct: each measure is aggregated at the query's grain and the ratio is computed from those sums.

options.text: As the average of North's stored daily rates
options.rationale: A metric view stores definitions, not daily rates, so there is nothing to average.

options.text: As the rate of the last day in March
options.rationale: Measures aggregate every row of the group; nothing picks a single day.

options.text: It cannot be produced, because the view was built at line-day grain
options.rationale: Measures have no predetermined grain; the fields a query selects decide it.

cards.prompt: What does a gold medallion label tell a dashboard author about a table's rows?
cards.answer: Only that the data was refined for business use; it states nothing about grain, keys or measures.
cards.explanation: Medallion layers describe data quality and readiness. A reader still needs the entity and a one-sentence grain, such as one row per accepted inspection, to know what a row means, which key identifies it and which columns may be summed.

cards.prompt: Why must a table's grain be declared before its columns are chosen?
cards.answer: Because every dimension and measure must be true at that grain, and a mixed-grain table sums silently to wrong totals.
cards.explanation: SQL adds rows, not meanings. Two inspections of 120 and 80 pieces plus a stored daily subtotal of 200 sum to 400, and the rate built on them still looks right because both parts doubled, so only a declared, tested grain exposes the mistake.

cards.prompt: In the inspection star, which tables hold measurements and which hold descriptions?
cards.answer: fact_inspection holds pieces inspected and defective per inspection; the line, plant, shift and date dimensions hold the descriptions.
cards.explanation: Facts record events at one grain with additive measures and keys; dimensions carry the words people filter and group by. Every fact-to-dimension join must be many-to-one, which a row count before and after the join proves.

cards.prompt: What breaks when inspections use line code N1 and downtime uses NORTH-1?
cards.answer: The facts can no longer be drilled across: downtime for that line looks missing beside every inspection day.
cards.explanation: Conformed dimensions share keys and values so separate facts meet in one report. A second code for the same line produces no error, only a blank, so the mapping is made once when the downtime rows are loaded, never inside each report.

cards.prompt: How do type 1 and type 2 handle a supervisor change on 30 March?
cards.answer: Type 1 overwrites the supervisor and loses history; type 2 adds a new row with a new surrogate key and validity dates.
cards.explanation: With type 2, an inspection on 27 March keeps the supervisor on duty that day (as-was) because the fact carries the surrogate key of the version valid then; with type 1 every inspection reads today's supervisor (as-is). Both are legitimate; the contract says which a report uses.

cards.prompt: Predict the row count when 22 inspections are joined to a type 2 line dimension on line_id alone.
cards.answer: 29 in the lab: each of N1's 8 inspections meets two versions, and N3's inspection matches nothing.
cards.explanation: line_id repeats in a type 2 dimension, so the join is many-to-many. North's pieces rise from 1,250 to 2,250 while its rate moves only from 2.16% to 2.13%, which is why row counts and parts are tested, not only the rate.

cards.prompt: Where should an inspection go when its line has no dimension row yet?
cards.answer: To an unknown member row (line_sk -1, plant UNKNOWN), listed for follow-up, never dropped by an inner join.
cards.explanation: An inner join loses the 50 pieces silently and a left join leaves an unnamed NULL group. The unknown member keeps totals at 2,440, names the orphan, and lets a later rebuild resolve the fact once the line is added to the dimension.

cards.prompt: Why can a unit mismatch look correct at line-day but wrong at plant-day?
cards.answer: Within one line both quantities share a unit, so the ratio is unit-free; summing across lines adds cases to pieces.
cards.explanation: S2's 10 cases with 1 defective case give 10% in cases or in pieces, but South's sum becomes 190 / 4 instead of 300 / 15. Converting both quantities at load, and comparing parts rather than only rates, catches it.

cards.prompt: Which parts of a defect rate may be summed across lines and days?
cards.answer: The defective and inspected piece counts; the rate is recomputed from their sums at each grain.
cards.explanation: Ratios are non-additive. North's line rates of 2.0% and 5.0% average to 3.5%, but its 300 pieces with 9 defective give 3.0%. An average of rates is a different metric that needs its own name and contract.

cards.prompt: What happens when a monthly target table is joined to daily rows on plant and month?
cards.answer: The target repeats on every day of the month, so summing or averaging it answers no business question.
cards.explanation: A join copies the coarser row onto each finer row: four March days make a 2.0% target sum to 8.0%. Compare the target with the plant-month rate, or apply an explicit, owned allocation rule if daily targets are truly needed.

cards.prompt: How should a line-day with zero inspected pieces appear in the report?
cards.answer: As no rate with a status such as no_units, never as 0% and never as a failed query.
cards.explanation: Spark 4's ANSI mode makes plain division by zero fail, and try_divide returns NULL. The contract then names the reason; a line-day with pieces inspected and none defective keeps its genuine 0% rate.

cards.prompt: Why does a business-day window need the plant calendar rather than a weekday rule?
cards.answer: Because shutdowns are weekdays too, and only the date dimension's business-day flag knows which days the plant worked.
cards.explanation: In the transfer set, Friday 1 May is a shutdown. The contract's window as of Monday 4 May is 29 April, 30 April and 4 May; a Monday-to-Friday rule picks 1 May instead of 29 April and changes North's total from 550 to 450 pieces.

cards.prompt: Name the clauses a metric contract states before anyone builds its table.
cards.answer: Grain, numerator and denominator over one population, unit, day, month and window, empty cases, unknown member, owner and version.
cards.explanation: Each clause implies a test: parts reconcile across grains, zero denominators give no rate, units are converted, orphans are kept, history joins on validity, and windows come from the calendar. A validator can refuse a contract with a missing or contradictory clause.

cards.prompt: Why does a metric view measure give the right ratio at every grain?
cards.answer: Its measures are aggregate expressions evaluated with MEASURE() at the query's grain, so the ratio is rebuilt from summed parts.
cards.explanation: Grouped by line and day the rate for N1 on 27 March is 4 / 200; grouped by plant and month, North's March is 22 / 1,000. No daily rate is stored to be averaged, but the join to the line dimension must use a unique key.

cards.prompt: What does a wide table cost compared with the star it came from?
cards.answer: Every correction or new attribute needs a rebuild, its as-was or as-is choice is frozen, and grain drift goes unnoticed.
cards.explanation: A wide table suits readers who want one table, so publish it as a rebuildable view of the star with its grain stated, test that its row count equals the fact's, and make corrections in the dimensions, never in the wide copy.
